title: CubeSat Micro Propulsion Nozzle Design

body.caption: Thrust vs throat diameter, half angle 30 to 20 degrees

body: This project looked at how the geometry of a small conical nozzle affects the thrust it produces, and one result stood out. Making the throat of the nozzle bigger did not always produce more thrust. Across a range of throat diameters tested for a CubeSat micro propulsion nozzle, thrust peaked at a throat diameter of 60 microns, reaching 2.098 mN, then fell to 1.787 mN by the time the diameter grew to 70 microns. The optimum sat in the middle of the range rather than at either end, which a simple scaling argument would not have predicted.

The project aimed to find the best geometry for a conical converging diverging nozzle used to extend the operating life of small satellite propulsion systems, where small gains in thrust matter because the thrusters themselves are so small. I built the nozzle geometry and mesh in ANSYS Fluent, modeled the flow as steady, isentropic, and one dimensional gas expansion, and set the boundary conditions using water vapor at 550 K and 5 bar as the propellant. Before trusting my own results I checked the setup against numbers published in a reference paper on CubeSat micro propulsion, then ran a full sweep across different throat diameters and different combinations of converging and diverging half angles, from 50-30 degree combinations up to 70-60 degree ones.

body.caption: ANSYS Fluent velocity contour at the optimum geometry

body: Comparing thrust across all the geometry combinations showed that a 60-40 degree convergent divergent angle paired with the 60 micron throat gave the best overall performance, with a peak local velocity around 1160 meters per second at the exit and pressure dropping from close to 500 kPa in the chamber to near ambient by the exit. The temperature contours showed the gas cooling sharply as it expanded and accelerated through the throat, matching the expected behavior of a converging diverging nozzle converting thermal and pressure energy into kinetic energy, so the underlying physics held up even where the optimum itself did not match expectations.

Nozzle design at this scale is not a simple scaling exercise. Picking the largest throat that can be manufactured does not give the best result. There is a real geometric sweet spot that has to be found through simulation, and for a system this small that sweet spot is not obvious from first principles alone.
